results.title: A Primer on Uncertainty and Calibration in Deep Learning
results.content: For example, instead of saying: *“The house price is 480,000,”a well-calibrated model would say: “The price is 480,000 ± 70,000 , but I’m really not confident because the location is novel to me.” And that ± 70,000 is where uncertainty kicks in.* Hence, uncertainty in deep learning is the **lack of confidence a model has in its predictions**, typically arising from **incomplete information, ambiguous data, or limitations in the model itself** (this shouldn’t be confused with confidence value model gives as output, though ideally it should, this discrepancy in expected and actual behaviour of model logits/probability/scores is comes under model calibration, this also will be covered in latter sections). A deterministic model makes a point prediction `y=f(x`), but a probabilistic or uncertainty-aware model outputs a **distribution** over possible predictions: `y∼p(y∣x).` Uncertainty is then quantified via: * **Variance**, entropy, or confidence intervals in regression * **Predictive entropy** or margin in classification That said, lets start diving into core concepts. ### Method 1 : Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) This simplest way of modelling this type of uncertainty is by predicting not just a mean output `μ(x)` but also a corresponding variance `σ2(x)`, treating the output as a Gaussian distribution: \(y^∼N(μ(x),σ2(x))\) During training, we use *Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)*, leading to the following Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) loss: \(\mathcal{L}\_{\text{NLL}} = \frac{1}{2\sigma²(x)} (y -\mu(x))² + \frac{1}{2} \log \sigma²(x)\) This formulation naturally balances error (left term) and uncertainty (right term containing `σ)`. Conversely, a model may express confident predictions (low uncertainty) but be overconfident and hence **badly mis-calibrated**. #### Ensembles and Dropout Both methods, discussed earlier for epistemic uncertainty, naturally improve calibration: * **Ensembles** smooth out extreme predictions across models * **Dropout at test time** simulates stochastic ensembles These methods reduce **variance** and act as regularizers, especially useful when used with temperature scaling. #### Prediction Interval Plots For regression models, especially those predicting both mean and variance (e.g., heteroscedastic regression), we can plot: * Confidence intervals (e.g., 90%, 95%) This reveals how uncertainty expands or contracts with input domain shifts, and whether **the intervals actually cover the target**, which speaks to coverage and calibration.

results.title: [1909.13550] Well-calibrated Model Uncertainty with Temperature Scaling for Dropout Variational Inference
results.content: Submitted on 30 Sep 2019 ([v1), last revised 18 Nov 2019 (this version, v3)]. # Title:Well-calibrated Model Uncertainty with Temperature Scaling for Dropout Variational Inference. Authors:Max-Heinrich Laves, Sontje Ihler, Karl-Philipp Kortmann, Tobias Ortmaier. View a PDF of the paper titled Well-calibrated Model Uncertainty with Temperature Scaling for Dropout Variational Inference, by Max-Heinrich Laves and 3 other authors. > Abstract:Model uncertainty obtained by variational Bayesian inference with Monte Carlo dropout is prone to miscalibration. The uncertainty does not represent the model error well. In this paper, temperature scaling is extended to dropout variational inference to calibrate model uncertainty. Expected uncertainty calibration error (UCE) is presented as a metric to measure miscalibration of uncertainty. Experimental results show, that temperature scaling considerably reduces miscalibration by means of UCE and enables robust rejection of uncertain predictions. The proposed approach can easily be derived from frequentist temperature scaling and yields well-calibrated model uncertainty. results.title: MC Layer Normalization for calibrated uncertainty in Deep Learning for TMLR - IBM Research
results.content: # MC Layer Normalization for calibrated uncertainty in Deep Learning. ## Abstract. Efficiently estimating the uncertainty of neural network predictions has become an increasingly important challenge as machine learning models are adopted for high-stakes industrial applications where shifts in data distribution may occur. Thus, calibrated prediction uncertainty is crucial to determine when to trust a model's output and when to discard them as implausible. We propose a novel deep learning module - MC Layer Normalization - that acts as a drop-in replacement for Layer Normalization blocks and endows a neural network with uncertainty estimation capabilities. Our method is motivated from an approximate Bayesian perspective, but it is simple to deploy with no significant computational overhead thanks to an efficient one-shot approximation of Monte Carlo integration at prediction time. To evaluate the effectiveness of our module, we conduct experiments in two distinct settings. First, we investigate its potential to replace existing methods such as MC-Dropout and Prediction-Time Batch Normalization. Second, we explore its suitability for use cases where such conventional modules are either unsuitable or sub-optimal for certain tasks (as is the case with modules based on Batch Normalization, which is incompatible for instance with transformers). We empirically demonstrate the competitiveness of our module in terms of prediction accuracy and uncertainty calibration on established out-of-distribution image classification benchmarks, as well as its flexibility by applying it on tasks and architectures where previous methods are unsuitable. ## Related. ### Sensitivity Analysis for Climate Science with Generative Flow Models.
